paras: The detention of Deputy Marshal Upchurch at Gibson's Station took place on November 2, 1888, in Richmond County, North Carolina, when a United States deputy marshal from Raleigh named Upchurch tried to arrest the local election registrar and was himself held by the registrar and his supporters. Upchurch later said he had been in danger of lynching by a crowd of hundreds, a claim the other reports do not repeat. Democratic papers, writing days before the presidential election, treated the episode as a "Radical outrage" that had rebounded on the Republicans.

Upchurch was sent by A. N. Shaffer, a United States commissioner and chief supervisor of elections at Raleigh, with a warrant for W. F. Gibson, registrar of election at Gibson's Station. According to the Rockingham Spirit of the South, which the State Chronicle called a "Radical organ," the warrant charged Gibson with neglect of duty. The News-Observer reported that Gibson had been reported to Shaffer by Deputy Sheriff Cameron of Richmond County.

When Upchurch tried to serve the warrant, Gibson and his friends demanded that he show the authority behind it, and he could not. Upchurch then prepared to return to Raleigh without making the arrest, but Gibson insisted that he not leave until he showed cause. A News-Observer account written the next day said Upchurch was "still at Gibson's" and reported "intense indignation" at the station.

Upchurch's own version, given on his return to Raleigh on the night of November 3, was more dramatic. He said he had been in danger of lynching all day and was saved from 500 angry people only by the speeches of Gibson, Gibson's brother and others, and that 300 South Carolinians had come over to help hang him. He was driven in an ambulance to Laurinburg on the night of November 2 and went on from there to Raleigh.

Upchurch said Gibson was to appear before the United States commissioner at Laurinburg. In Raleigh, Democratic chairman Spier Whitaker offered to join Shaffer in telegraphing that Gibson should appear before the nearest commissioner, but Shaffer first wanted to learn what had become of his deputy. No report of a hearing, charges against Gibson's supporters, or any trial appears in the coverage.

The surviving reports come from Democratic papers, and all treated the warrant rather than the detention as the wrong. The Richmond Dispatch ran its Raleigh telegram under the headlines "Republican Outrages" and "A Deputy Marshal Narrowly Escapes Lynching," alongside other items on Republican detectives and the coming vote. The Raleigh News-Observer, reprinted in the Durham Recorder on November 7, called the attempted arrest "an infamous and high-handed Radical outrage."

After the election the Raleigh State Chronicle mocked the affair under the heading "It Was Right Funny," quoting Upchurch as saying he was never so near death and calling it a case of "the biter getting bit." None of the reports gives the race of Upchurch or of the people who held him.

The threat to hang Upchurch and the crowd figures of 500 and 300 rest on his own statement as relayed by the Dispatch. The News-Observer and State Chronicle describe only Gibson and his friends keeping him until he showed probable cause, with the Chronicle saying he was held "a day or two" rather than a single day.

reader.title: Detention of Deputy Marshal Upchurch at Gibson's Station
bases: An election-season crowd detained a U.S. deputy marshal who had come to arrest a Democratic registrar and, by his own account, threatened to hang him; no one was killed or reported injured (A1, A2, A3).

No one was killed: Upchurch was held and then left for Laurinburg and Raleigh (A1, A3). The threat of hanging comes only from Upchurch's account as relayed in A1, and the News-Observer reprint describes a detention with no mob threat (A2).

Three Raleigh-sourced reports agree that Upchurch tried to arrest Gibson and was himself held at Gibson's Station (A1, A2, A3), though only Upchurch's account in A1 reports a crowd threatening to hang him.

accounts.gist: Upchurch said he was in danger of lynching all day, saved from 500 angry people only by the speeches of Gibson, his brother and others, while 300 South Carolinians had come to help hang him.

accounts.label: Raleigh News-Observer
accounts.gist: Gibson and his friends demanded Upchurch show his authority, and when he could not, Gibson insisted he not leave until he showed cause; Upchurch was left 'beaten at his own game.'

accounts.label: State Chronicle
accounts.gist: The Gibsons kept Upchurch a day or two until he could show probable cause; Upchurch said he was never so near death and was glad to escape with his life.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headlined it 'Republican Outrages' and 'A Deputy Marshal Narrowly Escapes Lynching,' blaming the attempted arrest for the crowd's anger.
The News-Observer, reprinted in the Durham Recorder, called the warrant 'an infamous and high-handed Radical outrage' and approved Gibson's refusal.
The State Chronicle headed its item 'It Was Right Funny' and called it a case of 'the biter getting bit.'
